notes: The visitors display mourning customs, including cuts on their bodies. The phrase linking their deaths to Gedaliah in verse 9 is difficult: it can mean “alongside Gedaliah” or “because of Gedaliah.” The account does not say that he took part in the killings.
The word rendered “eunuchs” can also designate court officials. Geruth-chimham may mean “Chimham's lodging place”; the traditional read form supplies the name Chimham.
vocabulary: Cistern
A reservoir cut or built to store water; here it becomes a place for bodies.
Remnant
Those left after the destruction and deportations.

notes: The speakers move from “your God” to “our God.” Jeremiah answers with “your God.” The changing pronouns remain part of the exchange.

Building, planting, tearing down, and uprooting echo Jeremiah's commission in 1:10. “Relented” retains the statement of changed divine intention. Verse 12 still speaks of restoration to the ground although the group has not yet left Judah.
The accusation is literally close to “you have led astray at the cost of your lives.” It can describe self-deception or a deadly mistake; the repeated pledge explains the charge.
vocabulary: Example invoked in oaths
A ruined people's fate could be named when calling down a curse in an oath.

notes: Azariah son of Hoshaiah is named here; 42:1 names Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah. The draft preserves the difference.

The installation holding the stones is uncertain: brickwork, pavement, or a brickmaking area has been proposed. The garment image in verse 12 may describe wrapping Egypt around the conqueror; another reading is cleaning it out as a shepherd cleans a garment.
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” Here it is explicitly in Egypt, associated with the solar sanctuary commonly called Heliopolis; it is not the Judean town of the same name.
vocabulary: My servant
The title identifies Babylon's king as the agent of the announced judgment, without making all his actions exemplary.

notes: The Hebrew shifts from the plural “kings” to “his wives.” The draft takes the singular collectively; it does not identify a particular king.
The sweeping denial of survival is followed by an exception for a few fugitives. Both statements are preserved.

The people and Jeremiah give opposing accounts of the disaster. “The women added” is supplied in verse 19 from their reference to “our husbands.” The cake expression may refer to representing or honoring the goddess. Several verbs in verse 25 are feminine plural, directing attention to the women within the larger group.
vocabulary: Queen of Heaven
A title used here for the deity receiving incense, cakes, and drink offerings. The passage does not give her a personal name.

sections.1: A word to the Judeans in Egypt

notes: This word is dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year, earlier than the preceding events in Egypt. The book has not arranged every oracle chronologically.
“The whole land” can also be understood as “the whole earth.” “Your life as plunder” repeats the image of surviving with one's life as the only gain; compare 21:9 and 39:18.
vocabulary: All flesh
A broad expression for living humanity; the scope is deliberately sweeping.

notes: The noun for “mighty one” has an unusual form beside singular verbs. It can be read as a warrior, a collective force, or a divine bull; the text does not name Apis. The draft preserves the singular syntax without deciding the identification.

The biting fly term is rare and uncertain. The poem shifts from a heifer and fattened calves to a retreating snake and a forest felled by an innumerable army. These images are kept rather than made into one literal scene.
vocabulary: Sacrifice
The battle is pictured as slaughter belonging to the Lord. The image retains the violence of the oracle.
Balm
A medicinal substance associated with Gilead; its precise botanical identity is not specified here.

notes: Caphtor is the Philistines' place of origin in this oracle. The Hebrew of verse 5 reads “their valley”; a different reading gives “Anakim.” The draft keeps the pinned Hebrew. Shaving and bodily cuts are signs of mourning in the scene.
The poem addresses the sword, then speaks about it. The second-person “you” in verse 7 follows the Hebrew rather than making every reference third person.
vocabulary: Sword of the LORD
A personified weapon addressed as though it could hear the plea to rest.

notes: “Stronghold” may be the place name Misgab. Heshbon sounds like the Hebrew verb for planning; Madmen is paired with a similar-sounding verb for falling silent.

The traditional read text has “her little ones” in verse 4; another reading gives a cry heard as far as Zoar. Verse 5's phrase for anguished cries is difficult. Verse 6's desert comparison can be read as a shrub or a wild donkey.

The words rendered “wings” and “fly away” are uncertain; alternatives include a marker or salt and going out or falling into ruin. Verse 10's curse belongs to the violent judgment oracle. It has not been recast as a general saying about diligence.

The subject of the ascent against Moab's towns in verse 15 is supplied. Verse 30's clauses about fury and boasts are difficult. The first-person mourning in verses 31–32 is not assigned to a new named speaker. “The sea of Jazer” is the pinned wording, though the geographical expression is uncertain.
Eglath-shelishiyah may be a place name or an expression meaning “three-year-old heifer.” “The towns” in verse 41 may instead name Kerioth, already listed in verse 24.

“Terror, pit, and trap” reproduce the sequence of similar-sounding Hebrew words. Verse 45 echoes the fire from Heshbon in Numbers 21:28, keeping Moab's forehead and the crown of the noisy people's head as bodily images.
vocabulary: Lees
Sediment left in wine. Moab's undisturbed life is compared to wine never poured into another vessel.
Chemosh
Moab's god, pictured going into exile with his priests and officials.

notes: Milcom can also be read “their king.” Ai's location here is uncertain. The flowing-valley expression in verse 4 may describe abundance or a valley draining away; the draft leaves the image visible.

The word rendered “discerning” in verse 7 may be read “sons.” The lion, pasture, and shepherd passage has disputed pronouns and syntax. Verse 20 may describe the smallest sheep being dragged away, or the smallest dragging others away. The same passage recurs against Babylon in 50:44–45.

The Hebrew has anxiety “in the sea,” an unusual expression retained here. Verse 25 includes a negative: the question can ask why the city has not been abandoned, while some readings instead lament its abandonment.
Clipping the edges of the hair identifies a custom associated with the addressed people. The reference is preserved rather than replaced by a general term for nomads.
vocabulary: Cup
An image of an allotted experience of judgment that must be drunk.
Sea of Reeds
The Hebrew name often represented in English as the Red Sea.

notes: Bel means “lord,” and Merodach is the Hebrew form of Marduk. The two designations concern Babylon's leading deity.

The heifer is pictured threshing; the rare form has also been related to grass. Giving the hand in verse 15 is a gesture of submission. The term rendered “foundations” can also refer to supports or defenses.
Merathaim and Pekod are geographical names that also suggest “double rebellion” and “reckoning.” The oracle uses their sound as part of its judgment language.

“Become women” is the oracle's ancient taunt about warriors losing strength; it is retained as the speaker's language. “Sword” and “drought” have the same consonants but different vowels, producing the shift in verse 38.

This repeats 49:19–20 against a new nation. The first arrival is third person, followed by divine first-person speech. Difficult pronouns and the flock/pasture syntax remain matters for editorial review.
vocabulary: Devote to destruction
The Hebrew destruction-ban term marks persons or things for complete destruction in this war oracle.
Redeemer
One who acts to recover or protect those belonging to him. Here the Redeemer also argues their legal case.

notes: Leb-kamai means “heart of those rising against me” and also encodes Chaldea by reversing the Hebrew alphabet. “Wind” can also mean “spirit.” Verse 3 has a repeated written word omitted in the read tradition and disputed “against/not” wording; an alternative begins, “Let the archer not draw his bow.” In verse 5, “their land” may refer to Israel and Judah or to the Chaldeans.

The military item in verse 11 can be read as shields or quivers. The final phrase of verse 13 is literally close to “the cubit of your gain”; a related interpretation pictures the cutting off of a life-thread.

Verses 15–19 repeat the creator passage of 10:12–16. Unlike 10:16, verse 19 does not explicitly name Israel before “tribe.” The identity of the war club in verses 20–23 is not stated; Babylon and an attacker against it are both proposed. “Before your eyes” in verse 24 may qualify the wrongdoing or its repayment.

Verse 30 repeats the ancient gendered taunt in 50:37. In verse 34 the written forms say “us,” while the read forms say “me”; the draft follows the read forms as Zion speaks as a woman. The monster's swallowing continues in Bel's mouth in verse 44.

Sheshach encodes Babylon by the same reversed-alphabet method used in verse 1. Verse 49's compressed wording can describe Babylon falling for Israel's slain or the further falling of slain people at Babylon; the draft uses the retributive reading.

Seraiah's title is literally “official of rest”; responsibility for stopping places is a likely sense. “They will grow weary” at the end repeats wording from verse 58 and is awkward in its present setting. It is retained, as is the closing notice before chapter 52's historical account.
vocabulary: Winnow
Separate grain from chaff by tossing it into moving air. Here the image depicts the emptying of Babylon.
Portion
An allotted share or inheritance; “Jacob's Portion” names the God to whom Jacob belongs.

sections.15: The Maker and the war club

notes: The dates and numbers are retained as this chapter gives them. They are not harmonized with parallel accounts in Kings. The three deportation counts, 3,023, 832, and 745, total 4,600.

The final group in verse 15 may be the remaining population or artisans. Verse 20's reference to bulls “under the stands” is difficult beside other descriptions of the Sea; it is not silently rewritten. The pomegranate counts of ninety-six and a hundred are both preserved.
vocabulary: Cubit
An ancient forearm-based measure. “Four fingers” gives the thickness in another body-based unit.
Lifted up his head
An image of restoring favor or standing; here it leads to Jehoiachin's release and provision, not a stated return to rule in Judah.
